title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation attack in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a news article depicting a conversation between two real, named public figures, an ABC finance presenter and the Reserve Bank Governor. The fake article promoted an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. No part of the interview occurred, and no legitimate publication produced the content. The failure is not one of a deployed AI product malfunctioning, but of AI tools being used by third-party actors to produce convincing disinformation at scale, with fake websites, articles, and reviews layered together to manufacture credibility.

The point of failure in the information chain is upstream of any platform check, in the production and distribution of the fabricated content itself. Catching it would have required either detection at the point of publication, meaning platforms identifying synthetic or fabricated journalism before it circulated, or consumer verification of the financial licence of the platform being promoted. ASIC's figures show the regulator removed tens of thousands of such scams in a single year, with investment platform fraud and phishing both rising sharply, which indicates the volume has outpaced reactive removal efforts.

What is not established is who produced the specific fake interview, how widely it was seen, or whether any individuals suffered financial loss as a direct result of it. ASIC's warning is a regulatory alert, not a finding of liability against any named party.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock has emerged online, exemplifying a growing trend of AI-generated investment scams. The fake article depicted an increasingly heated exchange about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never occurred, but scammers used it to promote fraudulent investment opportunities. ASIC reports this type of scam is rising rapidly, with deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians becoming increasingly sophisticated and convincing.

ASIC's latest research reveals alarming growth in investment fraud, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent, while fake investment platforms rose 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of most impersonated Australians, followed by other politicians and financial experts. Scammers create elaborate webs of deception using fake websites, news articles, reviews, and advertisements to build credibility before requesting personal information. ASIC urges consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers independently and avoid investments promoted by familiar faces with unrealistic returns.
